$\,$ $x$ is rational and $y$ is irrational. 

The negation of the composite predicate above is the following:

$\,$ 
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}{{field-3}}
questions.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$x$ is rational and $y$ is irrational" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(x\text{ is rational and }y\text{ is irrational}) & ≡¬(x\text{ is rational}∧y\text{ is irrational}) \\  & ≡¬(x\text{ is rational})∨¬(y\text{ is irrational}) \\  & ≡x\text{ is not rational}∨y\text{ is not irrational} \\  & ≡x\text{ is not rational or }y\text{ is not irrational}.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.problem:
Logical operations with predicates generalize the corresponding operations on statements. As a result, all the properties of these operations are held.

In particular, for predicates $P(x_1,x_2\ldots,x_n)$ and $Q(y_1,y_2\ldots,y_m),$ De Morgan's laws state the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(P∧Q) & ≡¬P∨¬Q \\ ¬(P∨Q) & ≡¬P∧¬Q\end{aligned}
$$

These can be used to negate open sentences containing conjunctions and disjunctions. For example, let's negate the following:

$$
n \ge 0 \:\textbf{ or }\: 2 \mid m
$$

Applying De Morgan's law for disjunctions, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(n\ge 0\,\text{ or }\,2∣m) & ≡¬(n\ge 0∨2∣m) \\  & ≡¬(n\ge 0)∧¬(2∣m) \\  & ≡n<0∧2∤m \\  & ≡n<0\,\text{ and }\,2∤m.\end{aligned}
$$
